Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Yesterday all Members of the House of Commons received a two-and-a-half-inch-thick binder containing a report by Senator Keith Davey and the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) on the supposed success of the six and five program. The Economic Council has just stated that the apparent success of the six and five program is, in fact, due to market forces, and not to the efforts of the Government's expensive advertising campaign. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That the Liberal Party reimburse the taxpayers of Canada for the cost of this report, and the cost of all six and five propaganda, on the grounds that it is misleading advertising.

Whereas the Government promised to implement a Canadian marine industrial strategy by autumn, 1980, and we are still waiting for that policy announcement; whereas during the previous two years over $1 billion in Canadian shipbuilding orders have been awarded to offshore competitors because Canada lacks an effective marine industrial strategy; whereas we are losing tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in industrial spin-off benefits because of the Government's continued inaction; and whereas the Canadian shipbuilding industry is facing its worst recession in a decade, I move, seconded by the Hon. That the Minister of Industry and Regional Economic Expansion immediately bring forward the Government's long promised shipbuilding policy, or make a statement in this House of Commons as to why the Government refuses to produce a shipbuilding policy and a policy to develop a Canadian merchant fleet.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The federal Government has not carried out its grandiose plan to provide low-cost mortgages for home buyers through a special tax-free investment fund. Nevertheless the same objective can be partially achieved by permitting municipalities across the nation to issue tax-free bonds for capital construction of utility systems as well as servicing residential subdivisions. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker):
That the Government bring forth legislation immediately to permit municipalities to issue tax-free bonds, to raise capital for needed municipal capital works projects, and thus generate jobs. Such a policy would use tomorrow's potential federal tax dollars to create jobs today.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET PROVISIONS ON PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister has gone around this country since October 27 and he has said everywhere that we would be relying on the dynamism and the creativity of the private sector in the creation of growth. Yesterday the Minister tabled the third set of Ways and Means motions since the November 12 budget. Except for minor alterations in those Ways and Means motions, the antiproductivity and anti-creative stance of the budget of November 12 still stands in place. How does the Minister expect Canadians and business to have confidence when he says, on the one hand, that the dynamism and creativity of the private sector is to be the engine of growth while, on the other hand, he files motions and conducts tax policy which is exactly the opposite?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET PROVISIONS ON PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET PROVISIONS ON PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like the Hon. Member to read carefully the Ways and Means motion which was tabled yesterday. I refer him to the numerous adjustments I announced in my October 27 statement which imply several hundreds of millions of dollars of relief in taxation to the workers of this country and to the small business community and the business community at large. He will realize that the measures and changes I have

December 2, 1982
Oral Questions
announced will be of significant help to the business community and the investment community as well as to the workers of the country.
1 also want to refer the Hon. Member to statements which have been made by spokesmen for the business community since my statement of October 27. These statements indicate that the changes I have proposed are positive steps which will help recreate greater confidence and encourage more investment. Therefore I invite him to rely on the words coming from the business community itself with regard to this matter.

Madam Speaker, the Minister knows perfectly well that the business community was counting on him to be a Minister who would reverse some of those terrible provisions. After he gave his statement on October 27 he indicated that he might do something with respect to soft costs which are incurred when a manufacturer extends his plant or makes alterations or additions to his plant, thus creating new productivity and new jobs. The Ways and Means motion filed yesterday does nothing with respect to the soft costs issue here. The Minister knows it is a serious matter. If we want to have advancement and growth, we must have some assistance for business. The Minister has done nothing. When will he come clean?

Madam Speaker, I came clean on this subject several weeks ago. I refer the Hon. Member to a press release which was reported in the newspapers of this country, a copy of which he has received, in which I indicated that changes had been made with regard to MURBs and to soft costs. These changes were announced a few weeks ago and also appear in the Ways and Means motion and will find themselves in the Income Tax Act which I hope to introduce next week.
Following those changes, the Hon. Member can refer to press statements attributed to developers who have indicated that the changes I announced will likely stimulate some $400 million to $500 million of additional investment in the construction industry during the course of next year. I think that is a very positive development. I invite the Hon. Member to refer to that press release and to the press reports on that particular subject.
Madam Speaker, I would ask the Minister to refer to his own Ways and Means motion. With respect to soft costs, it does nothing for someone increasing or expanding his plant.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN BUSINESS TAX PROVISIONS
REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN BUSINESS TAX PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The Minister knows there was testimony before the Standing Committee with respect to capital cost allowances. He knows that there are all sorts of innovative machinery that must be purchased, in the automotive and electronic industries particularly. Why does he continue with this half capital cost bankrupt theory of
November 12? Why did he not change the capital cost jurisdiction to make sure at least that those in high tech situations, those who must improve productivity to be competitive in the world, could take advantage of a fast write-off for their plant and equipment?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN BUSINESS TAX PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure that my hon. friend will be able to point out a number of provisions that I have not changed. Indeed I have indicated that it was not my intention to agree to all representations that were made asking for a tax break or tax relief right, left and centre.
The Government has to be responsible, and the Minister of Finance has to carry out his duties in a responsible way. I have agreed, as I said, to a large number of changes which I felt were appropriate in the current circumstances.
As far as the capital costs allowances are concerned, I examined this question very carefully and very thoroughly. I compared it with the situation in the United States, and in other countries which are in competition with us. Over all, our regime of capital cost allowances with the provisions that are contained in the Ways and Means motions, compares quite favourably with the regime that is available in other countries. I think this is good enough in the current circumstances.

Madam Speaker, the Minister says that the capital cost allowance system is satisfactory, but he knows that business profits this year from manufacturing retailing, et cetera are less than 50 per cent of a year ago, and a year ago they were terrible.
Why does the Minister carry on with this horrendous penalty against business and at the same time expect business to supply the jobs we need for our young people? Why does he continue with this foolish attitude expressed in last year's Budget, an attitude based on statistics that were totally out of date at that time and are now horrendously out of date? Why does he continue to penalize industry and business? Can he not do something to make his protestations around the country seem at least honest?
[ Translation]

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is referring to a specific provision in the Ways and Means Motion that was tabled in the House. It is true that corporate profits were down considerably during the past year. I said that it was a matter of concern for all Canadians, for myself and for this Government. However, the changes suggested by the Hon. Member will not solve the problem. What is needed is a solution that will stimulate our entire economy, and with it, the demand for goods produced by our manufacturers. The general drop in profits in our economy is a result of the present slowdown in the international economy,
December 2, 1982

and that situation is not going to be changed very much if we make minor adjustments here and there. In fact, even if I did take the Hon. Member's advice, meaning that corporate taxes would be removed entirely, even if I did, there would still be a drop in profits. In the circumstances, I think the suggestion made by the Hon. Member is irresponsible.

Madam Speaker, my question, too, is directed to the Minister of Finance. I am sure the Minister of Finance has received many representations concerning the iniquitous treatment of I.A.A.C.s and the capital gains reserves, which is still a remnant of the Mac-Eachen November Budget. Is the Minister prepared to consider any changes to the provisions governing the income averaging annuity contracts and, if not, why is he not prepared to entertain changes.

Madam Speaker, my officials and I have examined those issues very carefully. I have examined the representations that were made before the Joint Parliamentary Committee and also the report of the committee. I indicated in my statement in October that there were a number of adjustments that I was ready to make in the current circumstances. I have come to the conclusion that these particular provisions contained in the Ways and Means motion are the right ones in the present circumstances.
I would argue that the various provisions contained in the Ways and Means motion have been the subject of discussion and debate for well over a year. It is high time that Parliament came to a resolution of these issues. I will be very happy to debate those provisions when we come to the consideration of these issues, either in Committee of the Whole or the Standing Committee, if it is decided to refer it there. However, I would advise my hon. friend that the provisions that I have put forward are those which I arrived at as being the most fair in the current circumstances, taking everything into account.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary is also directed to the Minister of Finance. Since these provisions place a burdensome upfront tax, particularly on small businesses and farmers who in some cases are forced to borrow to pay their upfront taxes, and since this also has the effect of increasing the level of taxation by as much as 25 per cent, how does the Minister square his current position with his statement that he is going to rely upon the private sector and individual initiative, as well as the creativity of the individuals within the private sector, to generate the kind of wealth and confidence that are needed?

Madam Speaker, as well as trying to generate the required wealth and the incentive, we as parliamentarians have a requirement to try to
Oral Questions
have a reasonably fair tax regime. In the circumstances one has to bear in mind whether there are exceptional advantages given to limited groups of individuals compared to others.
As I said, a large number of changes have been made to take into account representations that have been received by the parliamentary Committee and by myself as Minister of Finance. I believe the current changes go a long way to accommodate the strongest points that have been put forward, but there are other issues and points on which we must proceed as has been proposed, or with some slight amendment.
I remind my hon. friend that, with regard to small business,
I have made several changes to accommodate and help small business, such as putting the 12.5 per cent dividend tax only on future dividends and not on past dividends, not elevating the taxation on health and dental care plans, and not proceeding at this time with the wholesale tax. All these provisions will be of great help to small business.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAY-OFFS AT BOWATER PLANT IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday we learned that 750 people in Corner Brook will be losing their jobs as a result of the partial closure of the Bowater plant. Considering that this closure will have a significant effect on the economy of that Province, is the Government willing to investigate charges made by people in the Province that, through its other operations around the world, Bowater is dumping paper products on the world market, and that it has refused to modernize the plant in Corner Brook over the last 30 years?

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAY-OFFS AT BOWATER PLANT IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will take notice of the suggestion made by the Hon. Member and examine whether it would be appropriate to have an investigation made of this situation. Indeed, if there are elements of evidence that could justify such an investigation, I will certainly discuss it with my colleagues.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Minister for the answer he has given. However, I remind him and the House that, in the 1980 election, the Liberal Party as part of its platform announced, and I quote:
Liberals will expand and strengthen the Foreign Investment Review Agency to include a periodic review of all firms ... to assess the performance of those companies.
The Mayor of Corner Brook said that they have been told for years that the company had been making money. Will the Government admit now that its failure to act on its own election promise has resulted in lay-offs occurring without us knowing whether or not they are necessary? Will the Minister

December 2, 1982
Oral Questions
also tell us whether or not the Government is ready to introduce legislation as it promised in 1980, before any other lay-offs occur in this country?

December 2, 1982

subsubtopic: MR. GREENAWAY-PREVENTION FROM PROFITING FROM CRIME
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my duty to present a petition signed by 2,820 citizens of Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in British Columbia. This is by far the largest petition that I have had the honour to present in the House to date.
The purpose of this petition is to express the strong opposition by the citizens of Cariboo-Chilcotin to the publication of any books and the reaping of any financial gain through the sales of any publication by convicted mass murderer Clifford Olson. The nature of the petition is to urge the House of Commons to examine what measures may be taken to prevent Clifford Olson from further profiting from his heinous and repugnant crimes through the publication of a book.
The petitioners hope that, in your examination of the petition, you will find the petition in order and that you will exercise the discretionary powers vested in the office of Speaker of the House to refer this matter to the appropriate committee of the House of Commons for full consideration.

speechtext:
Those Members were speaking of everything under the sun except Bill C-131. What they did say about Bill C-131, I must say, was filled with misinformation and allegations that were wrong and dangerous. Some Members stated emphatically that our legislation would affect universality. The fact is that universality is being maintained. Other Members have said that we are taking money from the poor. This is false because every pensioner who receives the supplement will have full indexation of both their pension and supplement.
Opposition speakers referred to the deficit, unemployment, Ministers' travel expenses and the Bill on public service pensions which is to be debated later. All of these subjects were lumped together to give people the impression that these Bills, each of which has its own intent, are directed against senior citizens.
I must say that the figures cited by Opposition Members were sadly out of date in many cases and, in fact, incorrect. Therefore, these figures give misleading information to the public about the impact of this Bill.
I repeat that pensioners who receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement will not be affected by this Bill. The majority of pensioners, more than half, receive the supplement and they

will get the full indexation on the supplement as well as the value of the full indexation of the basic pension. They will not suffer any decrease in their benefits. All pensioners will receive an increase in their pension as compared to the amount they receive this year. All pensioners, including those with excellent means and income, will receive an increase in their pension cheque in January, but it will be slightly less than anticipated. A key factor in this debate is that the Government has ensured protection for those most in need. This is the objective of the redistribution which we have always fought for.

In fact, the 6 and 5 program to be implemented by Bill C-131 must be accepted in order to stabilize the effects of the fight against inflation. And I think this is something the Members of the Opposition do not want. The Progressive Conservatives supported the 6 and 5 program to fight inflation, to cut it in half so that 12 per cent and 10 per cent will become 6 and 5, if everyone does his share. It means pensioners with adequate incomes, women with children who are able to manage, and that is only one-third of this group, taxpayers, Members of Parliament and Ministers. Our own salaries have been cut, and many Canadians are starting to follow our example and support this policy. In fact, we may be seeing the beginning of a success story. Inflation started to drop last July, and what is needed now is a joint national effort. The Official Opposition said yes, we agree with the 6 and 5 program. They agreed at first.
However, when it comes to areas where implementation of 6 and 5 is not as easy and where conversely, it is very easy to indulge in petty politics, then the Opposition all of a sudden becomes very stand-offish and will not have anything to do with these aspects of the program. It only wants to go along with the easy parts of the program. It has done nothing to promote the program and that doesn't need an Act of Parliament, and I am referring to the program that our Government Members and our Ministers and of course the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) are publicizing across Canada at meetings where they are urging co-operation by employers and employees and unions, many of whom have made a tremendous effort. As a result, a start has been made with reducing inflation and we did not necessarily need an Act of Parliament to achieve this. Now that programs are being used to continue the fight against inflation and now that we are asking people who are relatively well-off to do their share as well, the Opposition has withdrawn its support and is trying to sabotage this effort.

I repeat that I do not regret nor do I apologize for moving this motion of time allocation because of the repetition of the same speech, which concerned everything except the subject, or gave wrong information on the subject, which is only creating worry in a segment of our population that does not need more worries.
I believe that we should proceed with the Bill and send it to committee so that pension cheques will ar ive in time. This
afternoon we are engaged in a debate on time allocation for which I ask all Members' co-operation.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) should be ashamed to stand there as a Liberal and support this Bill. In true socialist tradition the Liberals will rewrite history. They have been taking credit for supposedly helping the poor for years so they can describe themselves as great Liberals. When they now have to cut back their aid as a result of the inflation which they have caused, they are trying to rewrite history by saying that everyone is prepared to support these cutbacks and no one will be significantly hurt. They say that these measures do not represent an abandonment of universality. That is not true.
We are proud that I 7 Members stood to give their views. Every Member on this side would like to stand and oppose the Bill but the Liberals will not let us. Only five Liberals found the courage to stand up and speak. Then when they stood, they were speaking for the Government. Were they trying to represent the views of 1.2 million Canadians, senior citizens, a substantial number of whom make barely over $8,900? Were any of the Liberal Members standing for them and speaking out? No, not one. Five stood and, in a mealy-mouthed way, tried to back up the Government; but they are so embarrassed that Hon. Members opposite with any sense of honour will not stand and speak for the Bill.
Therefore, the Minister must come in and impose closure. That is what we are faced with here. Let us not kid ourselves, this is closure. This is denying the right of elected citizens to stand up and say: "I have senior citizens who are being hurt". The Minister would deny us that right and she should not stand up and be proud of that.
The Minister tried to say that the six and five program is cutting inflation in this country. Nothing could be further from the truth. Senior citizens know what is cutting back inflation-the depression-because they have lived through it. They saw similar types of situations during the twenties, which then brought the country to its knees during the thirties. They know that inflation must be stopped and they want it to be stopped fairly. It is the depression which the Liberal policies are bringing upon this country. That is what is causing inflation to drop, not the six and five program.
The Liberals are closing off the debate because they do not like publicity; we are starting to get the point through to individual Canadians that this program is not fair. This Bill is unfair imposition on 1.2 million Canadians who are at the low end of the income structure.
Are there any cutbacks of expenditure of the Government? Has there been restraint on the part of Deputy Ministers who are making $90,000? Do you know what they will receive next year, Mr. Speaker? Barely 30 days from now, they will receive an automatic raise of $5,400. What are we taking from senior

citizens? We are taking away $209. They will make $209 less next year than they were entitled to receive under the regular system of inflation indexing. However, the Deputy Minister will receive an additional $5,400. We, as Members of Parliament, will receive close to $4,000, yet we expect our senior citizens to receive less than before. That is not fair. None of us stands here saying that is fair, but the Government is putting it through.
That is the state of Liberalism in the country today. Liberals are prepared to ride on the backs of the few. This Bill is just part of a triumvirate. They are even going after mothers receiving Family Allowances. Why do they not go after themselves and cut back their jet flying back and forth across the country? The other Bill upon which closure will be invoked, Bill C-133, is with respect to retirement allowances. It will affect seniors who have worked for our own Government for years, who have paid into the regular pension benefits plan and have also paid an extra 1 per cent for protection against inflation. They paid that 1 per cent, not out of their hearts, but rather pursuant to a signed, sealed and delivered contract. Our civil servants performed their end of the contract. They then retired in the fullness of time. However, the Liberal Government with the support of all its members, some of whom spoke rather bravely, will stand to support this cutback when the time for the vote comes, and the contract will be broken. The Government will break a contract that was signed. It has no sense of what it means to negotiate a contract, even though civil servants have fulfilled their end. speechtext: I wonder what the Speaker thinks of that?

Mr. Speaker, what do you say about that? What do you think of a Government that would do that? Has there been any cutback on the movement of these Canadian projects to the ridings where Liberal Cabinet members live? There is not one cutback there. Liberals will look one square in the eye and say: "If you vote for us, we will give you something; but if you do not vote for us, we will move that project out and put it in a Liberal Minister's riding". They have done that, resulting in extra cost of hundreds of millions of dollars across this country.
Are there any cutbacks on Crown corporations? No. In fact, it has been the very opposite. We now have a new Crown corporation, CDIC, which will require an entirely new structure of accountants, lawyers and administrators. Joel Bell will come in and will probably earn $90,000, $100,000 or maybe $150,000. The Government will never tell us how much it is

paying because it does not want Canadians to know. However, there will be no cutbacks on Crown corporations.
Have there been any cutbacks on sabbatical leaves? No. The Government hired a civil servant and paid him $150,000 to attack an industry, to destroy the only industry in Canada which could have carried us through this inflationary period, the depression. While all the rest of the world was mired in depression, we could have been strong. We could have been a source of capital and a source of energy to the world. But no, the Government hired a civil servant for $150,000 to destroy that industry, and then what did it do? It rewarded the guy. The Government sent him to Paris for a sabbatical, costing $200,000 extra.
Have there been any cutbacks on Government guarantees? The Government is prepared to guarantee the big boys who are prepared to kick in money to the Liberal campaign and all that, but it will not protect the little, individual Canadian, the senior citizen who is trying to eke out an existence in Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver and is earning nearly $8,900. Is the Government prepared to help that person? No way. I am sorry, senior citizen, but you do not carry enough clout. The Liberal Government does not like the senior citizens of this country and they will make them pay. They do not like mothers who have families either, and will make them pay. If one has a family in this country, one will be in trouble under a Liberal Government.
If one dares to work for the Government, if one dares to perform one's end of the contract and pay the extra 1 per cent, thinking that the Government will honour its contract, the Government does not like that person and will take it away from him. I feel very badly for any of the civil servants who are coming up to retirement age, because they will be hurt.
Does anyone ever get Fired from these Crown corporations? If Crown corporations make errors, or the management fails, are employees retired or fired? Never. In private industry we know that if 100 corporations start, at least 24 per cent will fail through inefficiency or bad management. Has any Crown corporation, in the entire history of Canada, ever failed? Never. That is because they come back to the Government which created them. The Government is into everyone's tax pocket and simply spends more tax dollars to keep Crown corporations going, with the result that there are now over 600 of them. That has caused a reduction of the tax base in Canada, and because Crown corporations are not paying their fair share of taxes, it means that the rest of us, as individuals, must pay more. Therefore, the Government cannot give senior citizens what they genuinely deserve.
When it comes time to show restraint and to try to put a program in place which is fair across the board, do the Crown corporations pay their fair share? No way. The Government goes for the poor little senior who has paid his way in the country. Most of these senior citizens fought in the war and many are now suffering grotesque disabilities as a result, whether psychological or physical. They need us more than ever, but the Liberal Government is letting them down.

There is no way the Government can justify moving to limit the debate on this particular piece of legislation today. This legislation goes to the very heart of the social welfare programs that we in this country have long supported. It goes to the very root of the incomes of senior citizens, regardless of where they live in the country and regardless of what their ability is to meet their financial obligations. There are hundreds of thousands of senior citizens in this country for whom any reduction in their income, considering the increase in inflation, will prove to be disastrous.
Yesterday when I spoke I said we were not only opposed to this Bill but we were opposed to any reduction of any kind. Not one single penny, not one red cent, should be taken from senior citizens in this country.

They were the people who came through the depression when there were virtually no pension programs. They are the people on whose backs this country was built. It is to them that we turn with pride when we look at the accomplishments that we have made in this country. All of a sudden we are asking them-no, we are not even asking them, we are telling them that inflation brought about in part by this Government's mis-spending has to be fought by senior citizens' incomes being reduced.
Mr. Speaker, I know that you yourself do not agree with this measure and I know that there must be, somewhere in the Liberal benches, others who care about the impact of what is happening here today. I know that there must be some on the Liberal benches who have an understanding of what this measure will mean. Not only does it mean a reduction in purchasing power for senior citizens in 1983 and in 1984, but it means for every single year of their life from today on they
will have less income to spend than they would have had and their income will constantly be behind the rate of inflation. It means that we have accepted in principle that senior citizens are not to be given incomes that even begin to meet the requirements exacted by an economy that does not show pity for those who do not have an independent source of wealth.
I say through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister, withdraw this Bill. Withdraw this action today; withdraw this Bill.
The Minister stands up and with tears in her eyes tells us that it is a small amount that she is asking senior citizens to give up, and it does not really amount to a lot of money. If it is such a small amount, why the hell does the Government need it? If it is such a small amount, surely the Government can find other sources of income in order to guarantee that these seniors will not be asked to make this contribution. My goodness gracious, we are looking for something like $30 million to $60 million over the period of time that this measure will be in place.
Is the Government saying that we cannot find that amount of money within the waste that currently goes on in various and many Government ministries? Is the Government saying that the information program of the Government is more valuable than meeting our commitment to senior citizens, so that they can have a decent income? Is the Government saying that the appointment of another 15 Senators is more important than allocating that money to meet our commitment to senior citizens' incomes? Is the Government suggesting that bailing out Dome Petroleum is more important than meeting the commitment to our senior citizens?
Is the Government suggesting that these small amounts that the Minister speaks about are more appropriately carried by senior citizens whose incomes are already inadequate, rather than carried by those whose incomes are far more than they need? Is the Government suggesting that it could not reasonably have asked those in the upper 10 per cent of the income earners of this country to carry some of the additional burden, so that it did not have to take this action? Surely to God this is not what the Government is saying.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is in my judgment one of the worst pieces of legislation I have seen since I entered the House of Commons. It stands alongside the worst legislation 1 have seen in 16 years of politics. It is completely against all the things that I believe, and that I believe that the Liberal Party believe, with regard to social justice.
I put to you, sir, that not only are we opposed to it, not only do we intend to vote against it, not only do we think that bringing it to a vote is inappropriate and wrong, but we think this Bill should be delayed by whatever means is available to every Member of this House to guarantee that the Bill never passes; and that is what we intend to do.

The Parliamentary Secretary should have listened to what the House Leader of the Official Opposition said yesterday. He made the proposal that if it was part of the package, we would deal expeditiously with Bill C-131 and allow it to come to a vote on second reading, in the same way as we would like to see the vote in this House on Bill C-133 to find out how the five originally honest Liberal backbenchers vote. I do not know how many of them are left now. I remember seeing in print that at least one of the supposedly honest Liberals could not vote for Bill C-133 in its present form. I want to be here when the vote is taken to see which way that Member votes.
If the Government had listened to what the House Leader of the Official Opposition said yesterday, it would have seen the opportunity to work together with those on this side. We wanted a package deal with the series of Bills dealing with the six and five program, we do not like what the Government is proposing and we want to have an opportunity to make improvements. We know the program will get through for no other reason than they hold the majority in this House. However, we had hoped to make some improvements to those Bills, perhaps improvements which you, Mr. Speaker, would find worthwhile.
Maybe we would have improved Bill C-133 so that it did not come back to the House in its present form and those who say they cannot support it in its present state could support it after amendments brought forward by the Conservative Party. That is not to be the case.
For some reason, the Government is scared of the NDP. I cannot understand why. I certainly would not be scared of them. I do not think they are any great danger to anybody. In fact, it is a Party that is self-destructing. I do not think they could take on anybody.
Today the House Leader for the NDP said this is the most fundamentally wrong social service legislation that has been proposed in 16 years, but how many Members do they have here? They have four Members here to deal with the most important piece of legislation in 16 years. They could not have kept this debate going and the Parliamentary Secretary knows that. That Party is so badly divided it is not funny. It is a Party that is falling apart.
I notice that Members of that Party are drifting all over the House, continuously leaving the benches of the Opposition and wandering over to take a back seat on the Liberal side. For example, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) is an ex-NDPer, and recently we had another illustration of someone wandering over from the NDP to the Liberal Party. In any event, Mr. Speaker, it is not much of a philosophical switch at all.
This, then, is the Liberal attitude which they show us today and have shown us on several occasions in the past where they needlessly imposed closure. They say: "Look at us; we are the rulers and we are going to show you people in the House of
December 2, 1982

Commons how we operate things here. We don't want you to debate this. We are tired of listening to what you have to say."
I do not know how many times the Liberals have invoked closure in this one session of Parliament. Not only do the liberal members have this attitude of arrogance towards the Canadian people and towards Members on this side of the House, but they also have that attitude towards their own grassroots supporters, and these people are rapidly catching up with what the Liberal hierarchy is doing to them.
A few weeks ago, here in Ottawa at the Liberal convention, the grassroots of that Party, what few are left, suspected that the Government was up to something and adopted a resolution designed to arrest these things which they suspected were going on. They adopted a resolution at that convention which told the Government to maintain universality in its social programs. I remember seeing the Minister of National Health and Welfare on television raise her hand in support of that motion. At the very same time as she was doing that, she was scheming underneath how to get rid of universality. This is the way the Liberal Government operates. At that debate, I remember old-time Liberals like Senator Croll spoke passionately of how they brought in the system of universality in the first place. They spoke of the parliamentary battles they had fought. They spoke with pride of the accomplishments of the old-guard Liberals of the Pearson era and before-before this bunch got in, Mr. Speaker.
Bill C-131, which we have before us, is the end of universality. That cannot be denied. All the arguments which have been presented that the old age pensions are still going to increase just do not wash. We are going from a system of universality in social programs to the concept of means-tested social programs. This is being done gradually. This year, the old age pension escalation will be capped at 6 per cent, but the GIS will continue to grow at the rate of inflation or a little better. Because inflation is going to be with us as a result of the deficit which the Liberal Government continues to run up, after a while, in proportion, the OAP will become insignificant in comparison with the GIS. It can then be discarded and we will have a fully means-tested Old Age Security system, if that is what I can call it-because, in my opinion, it will no longer be a security system.
The old concept of universality is that you pay in taxes or in various impositions, and automatically on attaining a certain age or succumbing to an infliction, you are entitled to the services which are there to be provided. Under the Liberals we are getting away from that universal system and going into a means-tested welfare system. We will all be on welfare.
The results of Bill C-131, in the long run, are inevitable and they are an integral part of the scheme of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and his predecessor. I can tell the House that Canadians will not be fooled in this matter. What is probably more important right now is that the Members of their own Party will not be fooled; they are going to turn around and vote against these people because these Party Members know what the Government is doing.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise this afternoon and talk about this time allocation motion. I have been concerned ever since I came into this House as to how we tend to mismanage our time. I wish to quote from the proceedings of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, where it says at page 7:7:
The purpose of parliamentary procedure is to enable a democratic assembly to operate effectively and fairly.
At the end of the paragraph it says:
As time is a limited commodity, parliamentary procedure should ensure that the time available for parliamentary business is used as effectively and as fairly as possible.
With respect to "fairly", we have had eight and a half hours of debate, 23 speakers from the Opposition and five speakers from the Government side; and in considering the speeches which have been given, I am struck by the lack of new information which is coming forward.
Time allocation is a good management tool. The all-Party Committee has just made recommendations which have been approved in the House in an attempt to streamline the legislative procedures of the House. It seems to me that time allocation is a method of good House management. It apportions the time effectively. I think it is important when you are debating a Bill such as this that it move quickly through the various positions, so that senior citizens are not kept dangling, so there is some assurance to them of what is going to happen. There has been ample time for the Members of the Opposition to get their objective criticisms across.
The Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) stated very nicely, I think, that time allocation is not closure but is a gentle form of ending the debate. John Kenneth Galbraith, in "The Scotch" in 1964, said, and I quote:
Only a thin line divides the articulate man of wisdom from the windbag. The Scotch expected a man to prove his wisdom by putting it to good purpose.
It strikes me, given the speeches from the Opposition during this debate, they are not really putting their time to good purpose. It seems to me that if they have some constructive criticism, the way to put it to good purpose is to get this Bill to committee where they can make their constructive suggestions and we can move the Bill ahead. In listening to the Opposition speakers we get the impression that they are not putting their time to good purpose.
Now, John Andrew Holmes, in an article called "Wisdom in Small Doses"-we are certainly getting that from the other side-said that speech is conveniently located midway between thought and action, where it often substitutes for both. When you look at what has been happening in this debate, there is no question that we are in this sort of nebulous position. The motion which the Minister has put forward this afternoon

December 2, 1982
Time Allocation
represents an attempt to move from the limbo between thought and action, from speech to action. It really represents an attempt to use the time of the House for action taken on the basis of reasoned thought and debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-131
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day when I spoke on Bill C-131 I indicated that I was not very happy about the prospect of speaking because it is a real shame that one has to speak in this House on such an horrendous bill. However, today I am very happy to speak on the closure motion on Bill C-131. I think it is a great privilege for anyone in this House to oppose this type of closure which has become standard practice by this Government during this session.
Closure is really an undemocratic procedure to enact in this House. I remember many years ago that I was disgusted by a Liberal Government when it imposed closure on what was known as the pipeline debate. That was way back in 1957. It was then that I became interested in being active as a Conservative. Therefore, on this occasion I am very happy to speak once more against this practice which this Government seems to have made a part of its regular bag of tricks.
In the late 1950s there was a fellow by the name of C. D. Howe who was the one responsible for closure. He was the C. D. Howe of "What's a million?" fame. With this Government, the phrase is "What's a billion?" And on and on it goes. For the past two days on this side of the House we have been speaking on behalf of a very large group of people in Canada in the debate on Bill C-131. But these people are a minority. They are our senior citizens. These are people over the age of 65 who receive Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement in order to support them in their retirement. However, two and a half days is not enough time for any group of people to oppose adequately a Bill which attempts to take rights away from a minority. Yet that is what this Bill is doing and it is why we have to speak out against closure.
December 2, 1982

The people on the other side of the House know, and they know full well, that it takes several days of debate in the House of Commons before word filters out across Canada about what is happening. I dare say that right now half of our senior citizens and half of their organizations do not know the extent to which this cutback will affect them through this program of six and five. I see the Minister shaking her head, but it is true. Bill C-131, in spite of the fact that the Government denies it, is lowering the income and placing many people on the poverty line who were not on the poverty line before. That has to be so because this Government is taking away the purchasing power of our senior citizens over the next two years.
It is all very well and good for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to say: "Thank God we will be in the promised world of six and five next year". If we are, the Minister knows the proper person to thank. But I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we are not in the world of six and five. The rate of inflation in this country is still over 10 per cent. It is still in the twodigit range.
Our senior citizens who are at or near the poverty line will have less purchasing power, which will place more and more of them on the poverty line or below. It is that group of people who are near that line who will be so seriously affected by this Bill.
This Bill does attack the universality of the old age pension scheme, which is the basic support for our senior citizens. Several Members have commented on this in the past few days and it really is the only remark that upsets the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Schroder), in a most incredible statement when he was reading his speech a few moments ago, probably written by department officials, said that perhaps we should consider that we should not speak in this House unless we can improve on silence. I suggest that is why over the two and a half days of debate only five Members from the Liberal Party have spoken. Obviously, they thought they could not improve on silence.
This Government has spoken about pension reform. The Minister has travelled across the country. I suspect she has spoken in every major city in Canada about pension reform. She advised us today that we will have some indication of what pension reform is all about in the near future. But let us take a look at the record of this Government, a Government that refuses to allow us to debate this issue so that the people of Canada will know what this Government is doing to its senior citizens.
In this Government's budget, the first thing the Liberals did was to penalize our senior citizens in terms of their savings and investments. The Government followed that with Bill C-131 and what it proposed to do via Bill C-133. This Government has done nothing to improve the status of pensioners in this country. I think our senior citizens should know that and we in this House should be allowed to inform them. It would be a far different thing if the pension system were in trouble.
Time Allocation
Certainly if this Government, like some other governments in the world, the United States in particular, were having real problems with the social security system, I am sure that Members in this House would co-operate in finding ways to finance what is an ailing system. For instance, our Canada Pension Plan is in trouble now. You can rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that we will give this Government the co-operation it needs to improve that system. But the basic support system for the aged is not in trouble. The OAS is working perfectly well. It is the kind of income support that any country would be proud to give their senior citizens.
This leads me to ask this Government and this Minister, why are they attacking this system? We recognize there is a demographic problem, but that did not affect Old Age Security assistance. We recognize that inflation is a problem in this country. But surely a government that spends money the way this Government has cannot place its problems on the backs of our senior citizens.
Let us look at what this Government has done. It has spent $13.7 million on Bombardier by way of guarantees. This Government has made a $200 million loan guarantee to Chrysler; there is a $500 million investment for Dome Petroleum; a $34 million debt guarantee for de Havilland; a $125 million guarantee to Massey-Ferguson; and a $20 million investment in Minaki Lodge. What about its recently set-up Crown Corporation of which this Government is so proud? I am referring, of course, to Petro-Canada, which is paying $18,000 a day in rent for empty space in Calgary. But now this Government is saying that it needs to fight inflation on the backs of the elderly.
My colleagues and I will continue to oppose closure on Bill C-131 as long as we are able. We will continue to oppose the Bill itself because it is highly unjust to the senior citizens of our country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to stick fairly rigidly to the subject of the motion, which does not concern the subject matter of Bill C-131.
I am a member of the Committee which has been reviewing the regulations of this House of Commons. One of the matters that we have discussed is the problem of getting legislation out of the House. The Members of the Opposition Parties that are represented on that Committee recognize that the Government has a right to govern, and the Members of the Government Party on that Committee recognize that the Opposition has a right to oppose.

December 2, 1982
Time Allocation
I do not believe that any Member of the Committee has suggested that opposing a Bill went to the extent of being able to block its passage other than by a vote on the floor of the House. Therefore, our discussion centred around how we can bring an issue to a vote on the floor of the House. One of the suggested changes to the regulations of the House that has been accepted and will be effective next year is a limitation on the time for speeches. It is hoped that this procedure will aid somewhat in the passage of bills at second reading. This change represents a step forward. I think it will be helpful to the Government and it will still leave all Members with the opportunity to speak. There is no restriction to the total time, but I hope that since speeches will be limited, the remarks of Members will have to be relevant because they will have to confine their remarks to a 20-minute package. After eight hours of debate, which will generally last for two or three days, speeches will be limited to ten minutes.
We have a very real problem which we must face. When I say "we", I mean all Members. The Committee had discussed the implications of our Standing Order 75 and I think it is worth quickly reviewing the three paragraphs in that Standing Order.
Standing Order 75A deals with a situation where there is agreement among the representatives of all Parties to allot a specified number of days to a Bill. A motion is then proposed and, of course, there is an immediate decision. In other words, the decision is made without debate or amendment. Under normal circumstances, one can also anticipate a decision being made without a vote.
Standing Order 75B deals with the situation where we can get substantial agreement between the Parties but not necessarily unanimous agreement. Once again there is a provision whereby the motion will allow for a fixed amount of time for the termination of the debate at that particular stage. However, since it is not unanimous, there is, in effect, a two-hour period for debating the motion, following which there is a vote.
That brings us to the third paragraph, 75C, which we are using this afternoon. Standing Order 75C deals with the situation where no agreement can be reached on time allocation and the Government sees that it is unable to bring an issue to a vote unless it takes this step under Standing Order 75C. In this particular case we are concerned with second reading. The desire of the Government at this stage is to get the Bill out of the House on second reading and into committee where it can be studied by the Members of the committee. This procedure, then, must be used because of the inability of the Government under the existing rules of the House to obtain what would ordinarily be general agreement that there be committee study.
The reason I am very concerned and wish to talk specifically about this issue is that, as many Members will be aware, there is a tremendous backlog of Government legislation. There are many Bills on the Order Paper at the present time which are awaiting passage. In addition to those on the Order Paper, there are almost 300-I repeat, 300, because that figure is very important-pieces of legislation which have been given
consideration in the various Departments but which cannot be brought forward because it is obviously impossible to get anything close to that amount of legislation through the House of Commons.
I know that you have a great interest in certain pieces of legislation, Mr. Speaker, so I will deal with those. They are also pieces of legislation in which I take personal interest. It is legislation dealing with the Public Service.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-131
speechtext: What does it have to do with the Bill?

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-131
speechtext:
The Opposition tells me to talk about the Bill. I am talking to the motion before the House under Standing Order 75C, which is to limit debate on the Bill. That is the subject matter of the motion and to which I am addressing my remarks.
I have been working here for ten years without success in an endeavour to get important pieces of legislation brought before the House. It is not because the Government is unwilling or that the Opposition is unwilling, but because there is an inadequacy of House time to consider these measures. We cannot even bring them forward for discussion, let alone pass these measures. Therefore, we find ourselves in what I consider to be the ridiculous situation at the present time where no matter what we do among ourselves we cannot reach an agreement which will make it easy for the Government to have discussions on its proposals or, for that matter, for the Opposition to indicate its stand on these measures.
I honestly believe that it is long past the time that we face up to the fact that far too much time is spent on second reading debate in the House of Commons. 1 fully understand the need for time to pass between the introduction of a Bill and its passage. I understand the Opposition's point of view that there must be time for the public to be made aware of an issue. However, I do sincerely suggest that this should not occur by dragging out a debate on second reading on the floor of the House.
When the Opposition debates this motion this afternoon, I ask them to address the subject, which is the real basic problem of when we must come to a conclusion on second reading debate-not passage of the Bill-so that we can get a measure into committee where we can call witnesses and delay it, if we want, to give the public time to consider the measure. We can have freer discussion in committee while we will not block the introduction of worth-while measures in the House on second reading.
I would be very happy to hear from the Opposition, particularly Her Majesty's Official Opposition, how they intend to handle this subject if they ever-God help us-become the Government of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-131
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to hear the eloquence of Government Members on closure, when they have more speakers talking on closing down debate than they do for the actual debate of the Bill itself in order to justify the extreme hardship they are asking the senior citizens of this country to bear. I suggest that the
December 2, 1982

sound of silence on this Bill would not be justified from the point of view of senior citizens.
We oppose closure because we oppose this Bill. We feel that there has not been enough time to make all the arguments, both from the point of view of our position and with regard to informing Canadians about the purpose of this Bill. It is extremely important that senior citizens and all Canadians have a chance to know what the imposition of the six and five program means as it affects pensioners by the indexing of old age pensions.
We also feel that the Liberals want to close down on the Bill because they have not really been able to justify their reasons for using senior citizens in this land as the victims of their economic disasters; and they have not tried to make many speeches. We think their action is unconscionable.
A few minutes ago an Hon. Member to my right said that senior citizens are the ones who suffered very much during the Depression, who fought to feed their families at that time, who have worked hard all their lives, have kept their costs down and are faced with inflated costs for their basic needs today. They are the ones who will be asked to bear the brunt of six and five restraint.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-131
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. May I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the subject of the motion which is before the House? My contention is that the Hon. Member is not speaking to the motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-131
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will agree with me that I am speaking directly to the point of the motion. As I said, the reason they are imposing closure is because of the very statements of the Hon. Member opposite. We feel the Bill has not had full enough debate and I am explaining that matters have been omitted and not fully brought forward. That is why we oppose closure, so my remarks are surely directed to the point in question.
I note the Liberals have not spoken to the issue of tax reforms. We feel that if there is such a financial problem, and indeed there is in this country, rather than curtailing the indexing of old age pensions, the Government should be considering tax reform so that those with higher incomes would pay more of the tax burden and those with the highest incomes, those in the very wealthiest sector of our society, should not have loopholes whereby they pay no tax at all. That is what should be done to cover costs, not take money from the indexing of old age pensions. That is why we oppose the closure that is being imposed on us today.
The other point raised yesterday in relation to Bill C-132, which has not been debated fully either, is that it represents an erosion of universal old age pensions to cut back on indexing in this way. We know that several times the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has been quoted as saying that he is not sure that we should have universal social programs and the Cabinet has been considering some rescinding of universality. Therefore, we want more Hon. Members to be heard on these issues.
Time Allocation
The Parliamentary Secretary said that there was no new information to bring forward. I am extremely upset, as will be the women of Canada, that the Liberals will not allow us to have a full debate on the impact of this Bill on women pensioners. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) knows full well that she has been sponsoring conferences across this land on women and pensions. Time after time, those in attendance have been told that women are the hardest hit by economic stress and the inadequacy of pensions.
The Bill will add a burden to the women of Canada. Over one million women pensioners live on very low incomes and most of them, far more than men, live in poverty. Single or widowed women live in abject poverty. They are isolated with no access to transportation. The high cost of living is hitting them hardest. They are facing a deplorable situation with increasing anxiety because their cost of living indexing will be cut by the Government.
Another reason we oppose closure is that women do not have adequate Canada Pension Plan coverage, and that matter will be debated at further length, 1 am sure. Many women either do not have Canada Pension Plan coverage at all or else it is extremely low since they worked for the lowest wages and are in and out of the work force because they raise children.
Women are also devastated when they become widowed. I am sure Hon. Members must know women friends who have lived fairly comfortable lives while their husbands were alive, but when these husbands die, they suddenly find that they are destitute. The worry which this Bill will add to their shoulders is quite immoral.
Many of the widows in this country are too proud to request the Guaranteed Income Supplement because they see this as being welfare. They have the right to a full pension which is indexed at today's cost of living. That they must pay the rising cost of fuel, must meet very high rents and costs of clothing and food which will be far above the 6 per cent increase this year, I am sure.
We also oppose closure because we have not argued enough on behalf of women pensioners, who live on average to 77 years of age, which is seven years longer than most men. They will suffer longer because of the cutbacks and the punitive actions of this Government directed toward old age pensioners. They are isolated by poverty. Many have contributed all their lives to their country and families as home-makers. They have raised Canada's children. They have worked with no pay or benefits and now they are receiving pensions. For the first time in their lives many will be receiving cheques in their own names, but the indexing on those cheques will be cut down. It is a disgrace, which is why we want the debate to continue and to hear a response from the Government.
Where is the Minister responsible for the status of women? She is not even in the House. She has not contributed to the debate. No one on the Liberal side has given justification to the women of Canada for the Bill that has been brought in or for why women will have to suffer from the cut in indexing.

December 2, 1982
Time Allocation
I would simply like to say that an article quoting the YWCA appeared in the November 11 edition of The Globe and Mail giving the reasons why the Guaranteed Income Supplement is not the answer and why we must have old age pensions for women above the poverty level. The NDP Task Force on Older Women, which has held meetings right across the country, heard from women who complained that they are not adequately served by the pension program of this country. I also refer Hon. Members to an article in The Toronto Star today which states that older widows are the poorest in society, that the cost of living is rising dramatically and that their incomes are going down. In turn, their indexing will be cut, which is immoral.
We want the debate to continue so as to give Canadians, particularly women of all ages, a chance to hear about it and to respond. We want to hear justification from the Government for why it is taking this action and what its impact will be on women pensioners.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-13I
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to take up a few minutes of the precious time of the House in order to support the motion of closure presented by the Government with a view to ending the debate. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Schroder) pointed out so perceptively, after nearly nine hours of debate, Opposition Members have had ample opportunity to express their points of view. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, not only are the same points being made over and over again, those same points have, for the most part, no basis in fact and are being voiced primarily to deceive the Canadian people, especially the elderly who are well aware that the achievements of the Liberal Party in formulating social programs and taking new initiatives with respect to social policy are quite exceptional, and if we look at what has been done by our hon. friends in the Official Opposition, there is no comparison.
Mr. Speaker, I am always surprised when Opposition Members shout rape when the Government, after a reasonable length of time, decides that debate has lasted long enough. After all, we were elected to run the country, and I am a member of this party because I appreciate its determination to do just that and, once the Opposition's arguments have been heard, to make decisions.
Mr. Speaker, in her speech the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell), who has unfortunately already left us, made it very clear that she had an abiding interest in this question. She felt that the Liberals had not approached the heart of the matter. Before the end of this debate, I want to say once and for all what the actual facts of the matter are, Mr. Speaker. I think we all agree, and no one is going to challenge this, that more than half of those who are 65 and over and receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement are not in any way affected by the provisions of Bill C-131, since they are guaranteed full indexation to the cost of living. What is the situation, Mr. Speaker, for senior citizens who are getting only their basic pension? At the present time, they are getting $246.92, which full indexation as of January 1, would have raised to $251.12, while capping indexation at 6 per cent will raise the present amount to $250.62, a difference and I think people ought to realize this before the end of this debate of exactly 50 cents per month. Mr. Speaker, if we calculate this over 1983 as a whole, considering that the projected inflation rate, according to the Government, will be I'h per cent, I expect that if the present trend continues and 1 have every reason to believe that will be the case, a senior citizen receiving only the basic pension will have a loss of income of $29 in 1983
December 2, 1982

and $52 in 1984. We are no way near the catastrophic prediction made by the member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) who claimed that on the basis of an inflation rate of 10 per cent in 1983 and 9 per cent in 1984-one wonders where she got her figures-senior citizens stand to lose $70 in 1983 and $220 in 1984. Mr. Speaker, I think it is important Canadians should know that between January and March 1983, senior citizens will have a loss of income of 50 cents per month, and this applies to 47 per cent of the population, while the other 53 per cent will be receiving the basic pension and Guaranteed Income Supplement with full cost-of-living indexation.
This is certainly not the catastrophe being predicted by the Cassandras in the Opposition. Mr. Speaker, people ought to realize that for this Government, the all-important thing is to win the fight against inflation. And it is important because we must not forget that many pensioners receive only the basic pension because they are already receiving benefits from private pension schemes which are often not or only partially indexed, and these are the people who will benefit most if we succeed in bringing inflation rates down as far as possible.
I would also like to comment briefly on what was said by the Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), who claimed that the Government was neglecting single pensioners and was doing nothing to improve their situation. I would like to remind the House that in 1979, when the Liberals were still in power-we did, of course, have that unfortunate period of eight or nine months in 1979-so before we were removed from power, we had increased the Guaranteed Income Supplement for singles by $20 and as soon as we were back in power, after the end of the Progressive Conservative interregnum, we added another $35. The increase for singles is the same as that for couples, because we realize that singles who are now receiving about 56 per cent of what a couple is getting, should probably get more, because as we all know, there are fixed costs whether you live in a house or a senior citizens' residence or an apartment. In fact, the cost of living for a single person may be about two-thirds of what it is for a couple. We realize we must do more for singles. I know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is very keen on this, and that as soon as economic and financial conditions permit, we shall act accordingly.
Mr. Speaker, in June 1982, the Minister of Finance announced that about $105 million could be saved by capping indexation of basic pensions. We are glad to see that the actual savings will be less, because it is an obvious sign that we are winning the fight against inflation. In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say it is high time we ended this debate. I think that within reasonable limits, the Opposition parties have had ample time to express their views, and besides, they will have an opportunity to make constructive proposals when the Committee meets for a clause-by-clause study of this Bill.

subsubtopic: CANADA COUNCIL GRANTS
speechtext:
That an humble Address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of any publications or items published as a result of grants given by the Canada Council to Mr. Bill Bissett.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the very refined language of the motion, I would in fact wish that copies of the material published by Mr. Bissett be put on the desks of every Member of the House of Commons. Perhaps if that happened we would have no more of the nonsense of publishing this sort of thing. There was no difficulty getting the books published by Mr. Bissett. In fact, they are available in the National Library of Canada. I have an armful of them with me.
Three years ago, in the spring of 1979, a number of colleagues and I spoke disparagingly of the federal Government through the Canada Council making funds available to Mr. Bissett. Mr. Bissett sued a number of us. I want it to be known that I would challenge Mr. Bissett to carry out that suit or to start a new suit, whatever he wants, because the material that he produces is simply garbage. I will give a description of it to a greater degree in a moment. I want it on record that I am prepared to go outside the House, where I have no immunity, and read this speech or any part of it, in case Mr. Bissett thinks that I am doing this in the House of Commons in order to be immune from challenge in the courts. I am not.
I fought for some time to try to find words to describe what I am talking about today. As my temperature rose higher and higher and as I read some of the material, I looked back at what some of my colleagues had said. I decided as a calm afterthought that I would read what had been said by one of my colleagues on December 13, 1977, just five years ago, when this matter was raised. I will read one paragraph referred to

December 2, 1982
Canada Council
during the "Late Show" when the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) was speaking. He discussed the material that I am discussing this afternoon and this is what he said:
This material, supported and masquerading in the name of art, is a demeaning degradation of human experience. It is in my view neither creative nor beautiful, it is not even grotesque or ugly beautiful, it is neither uplifting nor fulfilling, it is not even passionate or erotic; it is simply vulgar degradation of the human experience-vulgar and demeaning at a level well below that of funky graffiti written on the back of washroom doors. This type of vulgarity deserves to be placed in a category of the hate literature of pop art and should not be censored but rather branded as unfit for human consumption, and discarded on the rubbish heap to rot in its own vulgarity.
That as well as anything I could say describes the material published by Mr. Bill Bissett, yet the Canada Council continues to provide him with money. One might have thought that when this matter was first raised in 1977 the Canada Council would have had a look at what Mr. Bissett was saying and, as a result of that look, perhaps change some of its grants, but no. Since 1967, when Mr. Bissett received $2,500 to write poetry, up to and including 1982 when he has a short-term grant to write poetry, he has received a total of $53,274. I should be careful. There was one small grant to take him to Glasgow to the song and poetry festival at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada, where I hope he enjoyed himself.
I am not unaware of the benefits of the Canada Council or of its source. My memory tells me it was introduced at the time that Mr. Diefenbaker was Prime Minister of Canada. It was created to support the arts in Canada. That is a very worth-while enterprise and a very worth-while subject for the Government of Canada.
A number of people in Prince Edward-Hastings have received Canada Council grants. I have no fault with their grants. Let me go a step further and say that I do not pretend to be a critic. There are many things the Canada Council supports that I find of little value. My taste does not go to some of the avant-garde art. My taste tends not to be supportive of some of the literature, dance and theatre, but I find absolutely no fault with that. They are the chosen works of artists in Canada and are looked on as such. I would not criticize them. I am sure there are Canadians who support that train of culture.
Nor would I censor the work that is being produced by Mr. Bissett. Far worse than that, with the kind of garbage he puts out he is in fact stealing. I am confident that in any given year there are applications for grants from the Canada Council that are far more deserving than this. I am sure that if this money could be put towards such things as ballet, symphonies, books or dance, or any such worthy causes that Canada Council supports, I would have no argument.
If the Canada Council felt they needed to have an example of poorly written trash full of suggestive lines and four letter words, surely one example would have been enough, or even two. I will give some explanation of what is in the books. I will not hold them up in the House of Commons. Someone might be looking and would get a chance to read it, and I do not want to be responsible for disseminating that sort of thing.
In the books there are-I was going to say "explicit human acts", but surely they are not human. Surely the things described in his books are sub-human. The sort of thing which is described by Mr. Bissett in his works are beneath the dignity of the majority of Canadians.

Regardless of the protestations of concerned citizens all across Canada, which were completely ignored by the Canada Council, the pundits in that Department continue to fund this individual so he can produce even more of his so-called poetry which no newspaper in the country would ever think of printing. As my colleague from Prince Edward-Hastings stated, this man has received some $53,274 of Canadian taxpayers' money from the Council to produce his filth. Writers who write what people will not read serve no purpose other than their own self-indulgence. Let them write on their own time and expense. There is always the possibility that in the process of earning a living, they might even become better writers.
I do not think it is the responsibility of the taxpayer to support writers when no one will pay to read their works. For that matter, why should the taxpayer support theatre which no one will pay to watch? Tax dollars were never meant for the purpose of providing writers, actors or producers with an ego-satisfying outlet or income. There is nothing wrong with amateur drama groups, but I do not believe they should be subsidized by the state.
I have personally been actively involved for over 20 years in an amateur drama group in my own home town of Owen Sound, the Owen Sound Little Theatre. Not once has our group requested financial assistance, either provincially or federally. We have always stood on our own two feet, ever improving ourselves and our play productions, which has helped to maintain continued and active support by the people in our community over the years. Such grants, I believe, only

serve to smother motivation and incentive, not to mention desire and ambition. If it cannot be accomplished without grants, then it is not worth being done.

If publishers did not receive public money they would be more discriminatory about what they publish. They would really have to hustle to sell books and promote authors.
There is no question in my mind that art and cultural have always been part of human nature and will continue to survive in one way or another despite any intervention by the State. In other words, the people in Canada Council must take extra pains to live up to their mandate and trust so that they are never violated.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity of participating in this debate. It is ludicrous, to a large number of Canadians to see Parliament debating poetry when people are losing their jobs and their homes, and the country is in a major social and economic crisis. I have no objection to debating whether to give cultural agencies like the Canada Council money grants to carry on cultural activities. In fact, I wish Parliament would spend more time debating that issue. But for us to discuss the merits of a particular decision or method of decision by the Canada Council is a waste of time.
However, there is a larger question involved, that of censorship. When Parliament begins to decide what is appropriate and what is not appropriate poetry, then I think we start down the road of censorship, a slippery road indeed. I remind Hon. Members that it was a Conservative Government which appointed Mr. Applebaum and Mr. Hebert to write their report. The second recommendation of that report is as follows:
To the extent that the functions of cultural agencies and offices require the exercise of impartial, critical judgment in the support of cultural activity, they should be exempt from political direction in the form of ministerial directives of either a general or specific nature.
I think that also includes Parliament. The decision as to what form of art or which artist is acceptable is a decision to be made by their peers, not by Parliament. When Parliament becomes involved it threatens academic and intellectual freedom.
